TESLA ROADSTER FLIES, FLIPS AND HITS 60 MPH IN A FLASH Why Tesla Cybertruck production is winding down Musk made the announcement in a post on X, explaining that Tesla plans to use more of its Texas factory for Cybercab production. The move signals a major change in direction for a company that once expected the Cybertruck to become a significant part of its vehicle lineup. However, there's an important detail worth pointing out. Musk specifically discussed winding down production at Gigafactory Texas. Tesla has not confirmed whether it will move Cybertruck manufacturing elsewhere or discontinue the vehicle entirely. Texas is currently the only known Tesla factory equipped to manufacture its specialized stainless steel body components. Still, the announcement raises an obvious question. Why would Tesla scale back one of its most recognizable vehicles so soon after introducing it? The sales numbers offer a pretty convincing explanation. We reached out to Tesla for clarification on its Cybertruck production plans and what they mean for current owners, but did not hear back before our publication deadline. Cybertruck sales never lived up to the hype When Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019, enthusiasm seemed enormous. Musk reported approximately 250,000 reservations within five days. At one point, he suggested demand could support annual sales of 250,000 vehicles. There was plenty of excitement. But those early reservations required relatively small refundable deposits, and many never became actual vehicle purchases. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates, Tesla reportedly sold 38,965 Cybertrucks in the United States during 2024. That number dropped to just 20,237 in 2025, a decline of 48%. Things didn't improve much in 2026. Kelley Blue Book data indicates that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks during the first nine months of the year, down 28% compared with the same period in 2025. Those figures tell a very different story from the excitement surrounding the original launch. And then there's the price. Tesla originally promised a single-motor Cybertruck starting at $39,900 when it unveiled the truck in 2019. That model never reached customers at the advertised price. On November 5, 2026, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices again. The Dual-Motor AWD version climbed to $82,490, although Tesla paused new orders for that model. That left the Premium AWD as the least expensive version available to order, starting at $92,490 before additional fees. Of course, the Cybertruck offers impressive technology, including powerful electric motors and the ability to supply electricity to external equipment. But at those prices, buyers have plenty of other vehicles to consider. ELON MUSK REVEALS PRICE OF TESLA'S CYBERCAB Cybertruck recalls added to its problems Sales were only part of the Cybertruck's difficult journey. The vehicle also developed a reputation for recalls and manufacturing concerns. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla has issued 11 Cybertruck recalls since customer deliveries began in late 2023. Some involved software problems that Tesla could fix remotely. Others required owners to have their vehicles physically repaired. One of the most concerning recalls came in April 2024, when Tesla recalled 3,878 Cybertrucks because an accelerator pedal pad could come loose. In certain circumstances, the pad could become trapped by interior trim and leave the accelerator pressed down, increasing the risk of a crash. Then, in March 2025, Tesla recalled 46,096 Cybertrucks because a stainless steel exterior trim panel could detach while driving. That created a potential hazard for other motorists. The problems continued in 2026. An April recall affected 173 Cybertrucks equipped with certain 18-inch steel wheels. Tesla warned that cracks could develop around brake rotor stud holes, potentially allowing a wheel stud to separate from the hub. That could increase the risk of losing vehicle control. Importantly, Tesla reported no known crashes, injuries or fatalities related to that particular defect when it issued the recall. To be fair, these recalls varied significantly in severity and the number of vehicles affected. A recall alone doesn't establish that every Cybertruck has a safety problem. However, repeated headlines about repairs hardly helped a vehicle already struggling to attract buyers. And remember the famous Cybertruck unveiling? During the 2019 demonstration, two windows cracked when Tesla attempted to demonstrate the strength of the glass. That moment went viral before the first customer ever drove one home. Tesla is betting its future on Cybercab Tesla is making room for a car you may never actually drive. It's called Cybercab, and Musk believes these two-seat, self-driving taxis could become a huge part of Tesla's future. There's no steering wheel or traditional pedals. You get in, tell it where you want to go and let the technology do the driving. At least, that's the idea. Tesla began carrying paying Cybercab passengers in Austin, Texas, in September 2026. We've already covered some of the restrictions Tesla has placed on younger passengers. And while the technology sounds promising, there are still some important questions about safety. Federal regulators are examining how Tesla certified that Cybercab meets vehicle safety standards. That review has yet to establish any safety violations, but Tesla still has questions to answer. What I find especially interesting is how much Musk is willing to bet on this technology. He's scaling back a pickup truck people waited years to buy so Tesla can build more vehicles that drive themselves. That's a pretty big gamble, especially when self-driving technology still has plenty to prove. And I wonder how many people are actually ready to climb into a car with no steering wheel and trust it to get them home safely. TESLA TO WIND DOWN CYBERTRUCK PRODUCTION AT TEXAS FACTORY NEXT YEAR TO MAKE ROOM FOR CYBERCAB What this means to you If you already own a Cybertruck, there's no reason to panic or rush out and sell it because of this announcement. Tesla has not announced that existing owners will lose warranty coverage or access to service. Tesla currently lists a basic vehicle warranty of four years or 50,000 miles for new Cybertrucks, whichever comes first. Its battery and drive unit warranty runs eight years or 150,000 miles, subject to the applicable terms. You can review the details on Tesla's official warranty page. However, the long-term availability of replacement parts deserves attention, especially given the truck's specialized body panels. Tesla has not provided a detailed public explanation of how its production plans will affect future parts supplies. If you're thinking about buying a Cybertruck, consider how long you intend to keep it. Ask Tesla about service support and any outstanding recalls before making a purchase. You can check whether a specific vehicle has an open safety recall by entering its VIN at NHTSA's recall website. Resale value is another consideration. Limited production sometimes makes a vehicle more desirable to collectors. However, weaker demand can push prices in the opposite direction. Nobody can say with certainty where Cybertruck values will go. And if you're shopping for any expensive new vehicle, the Cybertruck offers a useful reminder. Exciting technology can attract attention, but long-term ownership costs deserve just as much consideration. Kurt's key takeaways Here's what gets me about the Cybertruck. Tesla spent years building up excitement around this vehicle. People put down deposits, waited for deliveries and ended up paying a lot more than the original advertised price. Now, roughly three years after the first trucks reached customers, Tesla is preparing to move on. I understand why Musk is excited about Cybercab. The idea of getting into a car and having it drive you home is pretty remarkable. But if I owned a Cybertruck, I'd want some reassurance that Tesla will continue supporting it for years to come. These owners spent serious money believing in Tesla's vision. I think they deserve some straight answers about what happens next. articles.body: A group of Western activists who travelled to West Bank on solidarity missions with Palestinians has been deported from Israel, the country's Population and Immigration Authority announced on Sunday."Fourteen foreigners who were staying in Israel on tourist visas were deported after being detained by security forces. articles.title: California shuts door on the billionaire wealth tax for which Google co-founder Sergey Brin spent millions but voters in two ‘AI capitals’ wanted it
articles.summary: California’s high-stakes, controversial billionaire wealth tax proposal is defeated. Statewide, voters are rejecting Proposition 40 by a 55% to 45% margin.
articles.body: California’s high-stakes, controversial billionaire wealth tax proposal is defeated. Statewide, voters are rejecting Proposition 40 by a 55% to 45% margin. The outcome delivers a major victory to Silicon Valley’s wealthiest residents, including Sergey Brin, and business interests, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into stopping the measure – even as voters in two of the state’s biggest cities backed it.Silicon Valley splits over the 5% taxProp 40 sought to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of roughly 200 California billionaires. Backed primarily by the state’s powerful healthcare workers' union, the measure was designed to raise money for healthcare and help offset Medi-Cal cuts for low-income residents. In the heart of Silicon Valley, voters overwhelmingly sided against it. Santa Clara County, home to tech hubs like Sunnyvale, Palo Alto, Cupertino and Mountain View, mirrored the state’s 55% “no” to 45% “yes” split. Wealthy Bay Area neighbours in Marin County to the north and San Mateo County to the south also voted it down.Yet the results revealed a striking divide inside California's tech and AI corridors. In San Francisco County, 55% of voters backed Prop 40 while 45% opposed it. That support came despite the city serving as headquarters for major AI startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are preparing to go public and mint a fresh wave of millionaires and billionaires.Meanwhile, Los Angeles County also voted in favour of Prop 40, passing it 53% to 47%. Unlike Northern California’s tech-driven economy, Southern California’s entertainment industry largely views AI-generated content as a threat rather than a windfall.Sergey Brin’s $102 million push and a competing banNo single person spent more to defeat the wealth tax than Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who contributed $102 million to the campaign. Overall, billionaire opponents and business groups spent $316.7 million to fight Prop 40.To make sure the tax couldn't sneak through, opponents also placed two competing countermeasures on the ballot: Propositions 41 and 42. One of them, Prop 42, is currently leading in the vote count. By prohibiting taxes on personal savings, assets, and retirement holdings, Prop 42 would effectively ban wealth taxes in California altogether.While Brin and his fellow California billionaires appear to have won this round at the state level, the broader fight over taxing the ultra-wealthy isn't over. Now Democrats control Congress in Washington, and lawmakers are picking up efforts to make billionaires pay more taxes, which could mean more pressure on rich Americans at the federal level.You use AI every day. articles.title: Restaurants bring back old-school hospitality as nostalgia takes hold across America
articles.summary: Ford's Garage president Billy Downs built his hospitality training program around his grandmother's warmth as restaurant chains rediscover nostalgia.
articles.body: After years of modernization, restaurant chains are rediscovering the appeal of the past. Pizza Hut has revisited its classic red-roof dining experience, while Cracker Barrel faced backlash over efforts to modernize its familiar image. Across the industry, nostalgia has become a way to reconnect with consumers who still have an affinity for the restaurants they remember. But as chains revisit vintage decor, familiar branding and throwback menus, some restaurant operators see an opportunity to revive something less tangible: old-fashioned hospitality. DISCONTINUED CRACKER BARREL FOODS THAT FANS ARE BEGGING TO GET BACK At Ford's Garage, a 36-unit casual-dining chain modeled after a 1920s service station, Billy Downs has turned to an unlikely source of inspiration for the company's hospitality training program: his grandmother. "We designed a training program that was designed after what a 'Greatest Generation' grandma would have served their family," the Michigan-based Ford's Garage president told Fox News Digital. The program, dubbed the "hospitality wheel," draws on the warmth and personal attention Downs remembers from visiting his grandmother, an approach the company hopes to replicate across its growing restaurant footprint. "I'll tell you this, she made you feel special, and that's what we want people to come out of this is feel special when they go to a Ford's Garage," Downs said. KFC UNVEILS RADICALLY DIFFERENT RESTAURANT IN MAJOR COMEBACK PUSH That philosophy extends beyond the training program. Downs said the chain places considerable emphasis on making guests feel welcome and fostering personal connections. "We also know that we have a unique dining experience in terms of the environment, but we want to have that hospitality be really important and we want people to get connected when they come on in," he said. That emphasis on personal connection comes as the restaurant industry increasingly embraces technology and automation, raising questions about the role of human interaction in the dining experience. Chef Joe Isidori, owner of Arthur & Sons, which has locations in New York and Florida, believes that as technology becomes more prevalent, the human element of hospitality could become an increasingly valuable commodity. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER A third-generation New York City chef, Isidori told Fox News Digital that younger diners are already showing an appreciation for restaurants with authentic histories and experiences that can't easily be replicated. "What they'll never be able to replace is the nostalgic real-life experiences," he said. For Isidori, the stakes extend beyond nostalgia. As consumers become more selective about where they spend their dining dollars, he argues that restaurants must offer something beyond food and convenience to justify the expense of eating out. "If they're going to spend money, it's got to have an experience to it," Isidori said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Isidori sees a potentially bigger challenge ahead as automation advances: ensuring that restaurants don't lose the personal connections that distinguish hospitality from a purely transactional experience. "Restaurants are really going to have a problem in 10 years," Isidori said. "I mean, the robots are coming." articles.title: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row
articles.summary: The culture secretary says the UK rejoining the EU's study and work scheme will help honour wartime sacrifice.
articles.body:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.

Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".

That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives, who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".

Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted that the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.

The UK is rejoining the scheme in January , six years after leaving it as part of the Brexit deal.

On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans who had died in conflict.

Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."

Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.

He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus.

"It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.

Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."

Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told the Telegraph that people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".

Asked about the criticism on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks.

"It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.

She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".

Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".

Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."

The UK is paying £570m to join the expanded Erasmus+ scheme , which the government said was a 30% discount. It will include free year-abroad placements for UK university students and their European peers as well as cultural exchanges.

The government said free train passes would be available for 18-year-olds to visit EU countries by themselves or with up to five friends.

Youth groups will also get to do short exchanges in other countries, with a focus on areas of the country less engaged by Erasmus previously such as the north of England and Midlands, the government said.

Applications will open for Erasmus+ later this month.

Farage described Erasmus as a "terrible scheme" and "wildly expensive" compared to the Turing Scheme, which ministers introduced in 2021 as a post-Brexit alternative.

He also criticised ongoing negotiations between the UK and the EU for a new youth mobility scheme ahead of a major summit on 20 November.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.

But the EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes.

Nandy said on Sunday that most of the benefits of Brexit promised in 2016 "have not been realised" and "there are trade-offs and choices to be made" on Britain's future relationship with the EU.

articles.title: Could Iraq’s Kurdish region return to two separate administrations?
articles.summary: A political impasse between the KRG and PUK threatens to break up the semiautonomous northern region.
articles.body:
Disagreements between the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) over the formation of a new government have led to the threat of two rival administrations emerging in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq, analysts say.

The dispute between the two dominant political forces in the semiautonomous Kurdistan Regional Government, which traditionally has operated under a power-sharing agreement, escalated after a parliamentary session was held last week in Erbil without the PUK’s participation.

PUK leader Bafel Talabani responded by withdrawing his party from the government, and a threat is growing that a rival administration could be formed in the party’s Sulaimaniyah base.

Independent Kurdish politician Yasin Aziz said the latest developments have deepened the historical divisions between the KDP and PUK.

“I believe the spectre of two administrations in Kurdistan is now very close, and the outlines of such a scenario are becoming clear. … The events have been painful and rapid. The differences between the two parties were significant and have now led to a breakdown in relations,” Aziz told Al Jazeera.

“There had been hopes that the two sides would reach an agreement, but activating parliament without the PUK deepened the divisions between the KDP and PUK.”

The KDP, which is led by Massoud Barzani, is the biggest party in the region, and its strongholds are in Erbil and Dohuk.

Since the first Gulf War in 1990 and 1991 and the establishment of a US-led “no-fly zone” in northern Iraq, Iraq’s Kurds have largely governed themselves, separate from the national government in Baghdad.

The Iraqi Constitution enacted after the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq recognised the northern Kurdish region as a federal entity with its own legislative, executive and judicial powers.

There is a historical precedent for the possible separation of powers in this region between two rival authorities. When a conflict erupted between elements of the KDP and PUK in the 1990s, the two parties formed separate local governments in Erbil and Sulaimaniyah, respectively.

While there have been no recent violent flare-ups between the two parties, political distrust remains deep.

During the sixth parliamentary elections in the region on October 20, 2024, the KDP won 39 seats and the PUK 23. This left a 16-seat gap between the two parties.

But the KDP’s ability to form a new government was still dependent on reaching an agreement with the PUK and other parties, such as the New Generation Movement, which secured 15 seats in the last election.

The PUK has so far refused to collaborate, so after a two-year wait, the KDP reactivated the regional parliament on Wednesday without its rivals.

Although the rivalry between the two parties is longstanding, Aziz argued that the current crisis is more serious and deeply rooted than previous political disputes.

“Given the political stubbornness of both parties, I do not expect an agreement or understanding to be reached soon,” he said. “Both sides must make concessions to each other. The party willing to make greater concessions will demonstrate greater concern for the Kurdistan region.”

Aziz was clear in laying blame for the deepening divide.

“The responsibility for deepening this conflict lies with the leaderships of Kurdistan’s two main parties,” he said. “Their failure to recognise the risks posed by continuing these disputes is one of the reasons we have reached this point.”

Subhi Mandalawi, a member of the KDP, blamed the current impasse on the refusal of the PUK to form a new government with the KDP.

“Following the Kurdistan parliamentary elections, the PUK delayed the formation of the new government. They were counting on the KDP being unable to secure the legal quorum needed to convene a parliamentary session,” Mandalawi told Al Jazeera. “But we held a parliamentary session without the PUK in 2018 as well, and they subsequently joined the government and parliament.”

Mandalawi insisted that the door remains open for the PUK and other political parties but warned that prolonged divisions would lead to deeper problems for the Kurdish region.

“Continuing to obstruct legislative institutions two years after the elections is unacceptable and harms the Kurdistan region domestically, regionally and internationally,” he said.

“Threatening to divide the Kurdistan region is a hasty, ill-considered and unrealistic decision. No party leader can take such a step, and the PUK would be the biggest loser if it went ahead with it.”

Despite the differences, there is little risk of a return to conflict between the two parties. “We are brothers, and there can be no fighting among us,” Mandalawi said.

Mahmood Khoshnaw, a senior PUK official, said the KDP’s decision to convene parliament without his party has worsened political tensions in the region.

“Activating parliament without the PUK represents a departure from the principle of partnership and from political realities, and there will be consequences. If a prime minister is appointed in Erbil, we will take the same step in Sulaimaniyah. Whatever the KDP does, we will do the same in Sulaimaniyah,” Khoshnaw warned.

“The situation in the Kurdistan region is heading towards chaos unless the crisis is addressed rationally and realistically. Activating parliament without reaching an understanding with the PUK has had a negative impact on relations between the two parties.”

Despite this, there are questions about whether Sulaimaniyah could legally separate from the Kurdish regional government.

Ramadan Albadran, an independent political analyst and constitutional affairs expert, said the dispute is not a constitutional issue about the KDP’s convening of parliament but a deep political crisis with the potential to create security repercussions for the region.

The Iraqi constitution also provides no mechanism for dividing the region into zones of influence between the KDP and PUK.

“If the PUK moves to separate Sulaimaniyah from the Kurdistan region, that would not be a legal or constitutional act,” Albadran said.

“If it takes place without a mandate from the elected Kurdistan Regional Government, it would be closer to an act of rebellion since there is no legal provision permitting withdrawal from or the dismantling of a region in this manner.”

articles.title: Bangladesh appoints Salahuddin Noman as new foreign secretary; envoy Siam to join Delhi Mission
articles.summary: DHAKA: Tarique Rahman’s government has appointed Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury as the country's new foreign secretary.
articles.body: DHAKA: Tarique Rahman’s government has appointed Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury as the country's new foreign secretary.Officials at the ministry of foreign affairs on Sunday bade farewell to outgoing foreign secretary Asad Alam Siam and welcomed his successor, Noman Chowdhury.Siam, who assumed office on June 20 last year, is set to take up his new assignment as Bangladesh's High Commissioner to India in New Delhi, a key diplomatic posting.Newly appointed foreign secretary Noman previously served as Bangladesh's Permanent Representative to the United Nations in New York before returning to the ministry's headquarters in Dhaka.Ambassador Noman joined the Bangladesh Foreign Service in 1998. Before his UN assignment, he served as Bangladesh's Ambassador to Nepal from November 2020 to December 2024.Over a diplomatic career spanning more than two decades, he has served in various capacities at Bangladesh missions abroad, including the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, the Permanent Mission of Bangladesh to the United Nations in New York, the Consulate General of Bangladesh in New York and the Bangladesh High Commission in Islamabad.At the foreign ministry headquarters, he served in several wings, including the United Nations, Economic Affairs, Administration, Protocol, External Publicity and Southeast Asia, as well as at the Foreign Service Academy.A career diplomat, Ambassador Siam joined the Bangladesh foreign service in 1995 and has held several key diplomatic and administrative positions during his career.Before his most recent assignment, he served as Bangladesh's Ambassador to the United States, with concurrent accreditation to Guyana, and as the country's Permanent Representative to the World Bank (WB) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).From 2023 to 2024, Siam served as Bangladesh's Ambassador to Austria, with concurrent accreditation to Hungary and Slovenia. He also represented Bangladesh at the United Nations Office in Vienna and the OPEC Fund as Permanent Representative.Earlier, from 2017 to 2021, he served as Bangladesh's Ambassador to the Philippines, with concurrent accreditation to Palau, and as the country's Permanent Representative to the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI).His earlier overseas assignments included serving as the first Consul General at the Bangladesh Consulate General in Milan, Italy; Assistant High Commissioner at the Bangladesh Assistant High Commission in Manchester, UK; and a junior diplomat at Bangladesh's embassies in Jakarta and Bangkok.At the ministry of foreign affairs in Dhaka, Siam also held several important positions.He served as Inspector General of Missions (IGM) and Rector of the Foreign Service Academy. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: How Ashley Moody survived the blue tsunami and emerged as a GOP star.
articles.summary: Ashley Moody defied the blue tsunami to hold Florida's Senate seat, and her rapid rise in GOP seniority could reshape the Republican future.
articles.body: Even in the face of massive losses in last week’s Midterm elections, Republicans had a few winners, and none may have longer-lasting effects than Sen. Ashley Moody of Florida who defied national trends for a GOP hold in the Sunshine State. Going into Tuesday’s contests, holding a Senate seat in Florida may have seemed like the least Republicans could do, but it turned out to be a night where the least they could do was the most they did, and those who did win should be learned from. "I fought tooth and nail this election to make sure Floridians know that what we have here is special, and it can be dismantled in one cycle," Moody told Fox News Digital in the wake of the blue tsunami, and while that message faltered in states like Texas, in Florida it stuck. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' Moody said her campaign held to two basic messages. "Talking to folks on the ground and meeting them where they were was vital, and I heard many people from all political backgrounds present a consistent message – they want a government that is accountable and a government that protects their pursuit of the American Dream. I put that front and center in my campaign and Floridians backed me for it." Accountability and the American dream: These are two very good places to start as the GOP licks its wounds and seeks a path back to power on Capitol Hill having squandered both houses in this cycle. DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED Many have been tempted to dismiss Moody’s victory by saying, "but it's red Florida." But red Texas turned bluer than the Gulf of America. So no, Florida did not carry Ashley Moody. Ashley Moody helped carry Florida. Moody was twice elected statewide as attorney general, first in 2018 by low single digits, then in 2022 by a whopping 21% of the vote, and unlike Ken Paxton, the Texas AG who lost his Senate bid last week, Moody did not have a long resume of scandal to bog her down. Moody also outperformed South Carolina Sen. Darlene Graham, who took over the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham after he died earlier this year, a decision driven by President Donald Trump that many believe cost Republicans the Palmetto state seat. Now, in the new Congress, Republicans will end up having lost between seven and nine seats. What this means for Moody is a fast track to seniority. With GOP Senate stalwarts like John Cornyn of Texas and Susan Collins of Maine having lost this cycle, Moody has jumped significantly ahead in line. MASSIVE UPSET: ANDREWS DOWNS TRUMP-BACKED GRAHAM IN RUBY-RED SOUTH CAROLINA Although Moody is just as much responsible for Republican success in Florida - which also included the election of Rep. Byron Donalds as governor - as Republican success in Florida is for Moody, one would be remiss not to mention current Gov. Ron DeSantis, the architect of the so-called ‘free state of Florida." DeSantis has built a GOP brand in Florida that is laser focused on the two issues Moody credited for her victory, government accountability and saving the American dream for the next generation. DeSantis made his state a beacon for conservatives across America who came in droves from places like New York City, now, it may become a lighthouse, guiding a national Republican Party adrift at sea back to the shores of electoral victory. Of the GOP wipeout, DeSantis said, "A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate. That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it." This is noticeably at odds with Vice President JD Vance’s theory of the loss, which states that GOP voters did in fact come out, but voted for Democrats, mainly because of the war in Iran and our nation’s relationship with Israel. Figuring out which of these theories is true, or at least dominant, is the first order of business for Republicans looking to regroup, and it is worth noting that while the GOP lost Vance’s old Senate seat in Ohio, Moody held Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Florida seat intact. articles.title: Egypt’s reopening of its embassy in Tripoli signals regional shift on Libya
articles.summary: Former rivals in Libya are pushing for a unity government to end years of conflict.
articles.body:
The reopening of the Egyptian embassy in Tripoli marks a fundamental political shift, both domestically and regionally, for Libya, analysts say.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty inaugurated the historic embassy building on Saturday, which had been closed for 12 years due to security concerns.

Libya has been politically divided since the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, with rival administrations formed in Tripoli in the west and Tobruk and Benghazi in the east.

Egypt was widely considered to be backing the eastern authority, effectively led by strongman and renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, and his self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA), until recent regional developments led Cairo to rethink its approach.

Libyan political analyst Hazem al-Rayes said the reopening of the embassy in Tripoli – which was the seat of the internationally recognised government that Haftar was fighting – is a sign of this.

“I can consider that what Egypt is doing in its recent moves towards the capital, Tripoli, is an attempt to readjust its behaviour in the Libyan file … [for] five years, no Egyptian foreign minister visited the capital,” he told Al Jazeera.

Elias al-Barouni, a political science professor at Libya’s Nalut University, also believes the move goes beyond the resumption of regular consular services in Tripoli.

“We are facing an indicator of a shift in Cairo’s method of managing its relations with the Libyan parties, and a rearrangement of its priorities in dealing with the Libyan crisis,” al-Barouni told Al Jazeera.

There have been several significant political and regional shifts that have somewhat stabilised the volatile situation in Libya, where thousands have been killed in fighting between militias attached to rival political authorities.

In July 2026, Ankara and the LNA reached unprecedented coordination , spearheading agreements to develop military facilities, advanced surveillance systems, and training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers.

The deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces and Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, has also paid visits to regional capitals, including Turkiye and Qatar, which have supported the United Nations-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) in Tripoli.

In Libya, rivals recently signed the so-called “4+4 agreement” that sets out a roadmap for possible presidential and legislative elections over the next two years.

Badr Hassan al-Shafei, a professor of African studies and conflict resolution at Cairo University, told Al Jazeera that Egypt came to revisit its policy towards Libya after realising that its reliance on eastern forces, led by Haftar, was not conducive to its overall strategic interests.

“It is clear that Cairo … found that relying on one party or leaning towards one party in Libya, which is Haftar’s party, may not be the right bet perhaps at the present time or even for a while, since the Turkish intervention several years ago,” al-Shafei told Al Jazeera.

“Consequently, perhaps Egypt wants to create a balance or also send a message to Haftar that he should not act unilaterally and that acting should be in coordination with Cairo, so it worked to extend bridges of cooperation with Libya also …”

Egypt has also become more concerned about developments to the south of its border, particularly the expansion of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, which had allegedly received support from Haftar .

“Today, Egypt is no longer the Egypt of five years ago when its policies and relations were limited only to the [eastern] authorities in Benghazi,” al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

It is “convinced today that its ally [LNA], which it supported throughout the past years at the expense of the legitimate government in Tripoli … has distanced itself from it today, and it needs to readjust its political behaviour with Tripoli and with the legitimate government”, he said.

During Abdelatty’s visit to Tripoli, he discussed critical economic files with Libyan officials, including the 2019 maritime border memorandum of understanding signed between Tripoli and Ankara.

According to the Facebook page of the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Abdelatty reaffirmed the importance of addressing Egyptian concerns regarding maritime demarcation between Libya and Turkiye in light of international law. The eastern parliament recently ratified the maritime agreement, which it initially opposed.

“Consequently, perhaps Cairo is trying to prevent the ratification of this agreement from causing damage to its interests in gas and oil exploration in the Eastern Mediterranean, and from that it wanted to extend bridges to Tripoli as well,” al-Shafei said.

“Instead of limiting itself to political and diplomatic objection from outside Tripoli, Cairo has become negotiating directly with the Libyan government that signed the agreement.”

Egypt might also be attracted to opportunities that reconstruction and the revival of Libya’s oil industry might bring.

“Perhaps with the reconstruction process, the incoming Egyptian labour will have priority, or even the currently present one will have its living conditions improved, not to mention the idea of the possibility of Egyptian investments and companies entering the reconstruction process,” al-Shafei said.

After years of backing rival sides, a new regional consensus means there is a greater likelihood of rivals in Libya reaching a comprehensive agreement to end the war, al-Rayes told Al Jazeera.

But al-Barouni cautioned that there is still a plethora of issues facing Libya, and only a comprehensive solution can end the divisions within Libya.

“The Libyan problem is not merely a dispute over the name of the head of government, but rather it is a dispute over the nature of power, the distribution of influence, control over institutions and resources, the future of the military institution, and the conditions for reaching elections,” al-Barouni said.

“If Cairo, Ankara, Washington, and other capitals agree on the necessity of ending the division, that is a development that can be built upon, but the success of any settlement remains linked to the ability of the Libyans to formulate an independent national project. Libya needs a settlement that ends the division, not a deal that redistributes the division.”

articles.title: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged by falling debris after attempted attack, ministry says
articles.summary: RIYADH — An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on ​Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom’s Energy Ministry said.
articles.body: RIYADH — An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on ​Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom’s Energy Ministry said. A witness reported blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital’s King Abdullah Financial District. The incident, which the ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said ​it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis towards Riyadh. Aramco was not ​immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the ⁠Houthis. Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly ​after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities ​later announced that the danger had passed. The Saudi-led coalition that has been fighting the Houthis subsequently said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the kingdom’s southern region. The Houthis have stepped up missile and ​drone attacks on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities since fighting resumed in July and ​became another front in the wider Middle East war reignited following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in ‌February. Saudi ⁠Arabia has carried out airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen. Alerts in oil-rich eastern province Earlier on Sunday, Saudi Civil Defense issued and later lifted warnings in several areas of the oil-rich Eastern Province, including Dhahran, home to the headquarters of state oil giant Saudi Aramco. The Eastern Province holds ​most of the kingdom’s ​oil and gas reserves. ⁠Saudi Aramco’s headquarters suffered extensive damage in an attack in October. An attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on October 10 killed 13 people ​and wounded more than 300, according to Saudi authorities. The renewed hostilities ​have shattered ⁠a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted fighting between the two sides. Saudi Arabia led a coalition of Arab states into Yemen in 2015 to restore the internationally recognised government after the Houthis ⁠seized the ​capital Sanaa. The latest escalation comes a day after Yemen’s ​Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes killed at least 33 people near Sanaa. Saudi authorities said they were investigating.

articles.title: Blue Angels pilot removed from team for 'failing to uphold' standards, Navy says
articles.summary: Blue Angels pilot Scott Laux was removed for failing to uphold team standards, forcing the squadron to fly five jets at its Pensacola season finale.
articles.body: A Blue Angels pilot was removed from the Navy’s flight demonstration team for "failing to uphold" its standards, leaving squadron with a five-jet show on Friday. The dismissal comes just months after a controversial low Pensacola Beach flyover in July that sent debris flying, raising concern for public safety. Maj. Scott Laux, a second-year member of the elite team, was identified as Blue Angel No. 6. The Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) confirmed his removal to the Pensacola News Journal, saying the decision was announced Friday before the season finale at home in Pensacola. NAVY SAYS NO REPRIMANDS OR FIRINGS AFTER BLUE ANGELS’ LOW PASS OVER BEACHGOERS "Blue Angel #6 was removed from the team for failing to uphold the standards expected of members of the Navy Flight Demonstration Squadron and will not participate in the team’s remaining performance this season," Chief of Naval Air Training (CNATRA) public affairs office wrote in a statement Friday. When reached for comment, CNATRA noted Sunday the removal came Nov. 3. Laux previously defended the team’s low-flying displays after the July flyover over Pensacola Beach sent tents, beach chairs and umbrellas flying as sand swept across the shoreline. "We appreciate the trust in support and it’s our privilege to be able to perform in that way," Laux told Rolling with Madrina after the incident. "We’re gonna keep bringing the heat and continue doing it safely." VIRAL VIDEO OF JETS BUZZING DHL STADIUM IN CAPE TOWN PROMPTS AVIATION SAFETY INVESTIGATION Navy and War Department leaders had previously defended the low flyovers. "Flight debrief complete. No reprimands. No firings. No problem," acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X in July. "That’s the sound of Freedom! Semper fi and Hooyah." War Secretary Pete Hegseth had vowed more support. "The flyovers will continue until morale improves," Hegseth wrote on X. The White House posted a photo meme of the controversial flyover from its official X account. "It's okay to love America," the post read. HEGSETH STEPS IN TO ‘FIX’ SITUATION AFTER APACHE PILOTS SUSPENDED FOR ‘SALUTE FROM THE SHORES’ FLYOVER The Navy has not said when Laux was dismissed or what conduct prompted the decision. His photo and biography are no longer featured on the Blue Angels’ website's team page. Laux was absent from the squadron’s NAS Pensacola Homecoming Air Show on Friday and Saturday, where the team performed with five jets instead of its usual six. Laux's role was the opposing solo, which flies with lead solo #5 in the head-on crossing passes and mirror-image maneuvers that fill the gaps between the four-jet Diamond’s routines. The routines were adjusted to account for the missing jet, according to reports. The 2026 narrator, Lt. Cmdr. Ronny Hafeza, might replace Laux on the 2027 team. The Blue Angels officers serve three-year terms, one as a narrator as Laux did. Laux, a native of Chantilly, Va., graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 2012 with a degree in Chinese and earned his wings in 2015, according to his bio, which as of Sunday morning could still be accessed on the site despite no longer being listed with the rest of the team. He flew F/A-18 Hornets with Marine Corps squadrons, deployed to Japan and aboard the USS Nimitz and supported three operations during the 2020 carrier deployment: Resolute Support, Inherent Resolve and Octave Quartz. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He later transitioned to the F-35C Lightning II and served as an instructor pilot before joining the Blue Angels in September 2024. Before becoming Blue Angels #6, he served as the show's narrator. Laux has more than 1,300 flight hours and 169 aircraft carrier landings. His awards include two Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medals and multiple unit awards.

articles.title: At least 21 dead as small boat sinks off Senegal
articles.summary: Senegalese Interior Ministry says one person rescued as search operation continues after migrant vessel capsized.
articles.body:
A small boat carrying migrants and refugees has sunk off northwestern Senegal, killing at least 21 people.

The Senegalese Interior Ministry said in a statement on Sunday that one person had been rescued in addition to the 21 bodies recovered.

The ministry said the death toll was “provisional” as of late Saturday, adding that the search was still ongoing and the families of the victims were being helped.

Media reports said the pirogue-type flat-bottomed boat capsized on Saturday off the Loumpoul dunes in the Kebemer department, between Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis.

Le Soleil newspaper said that most of the victims were from the Leona and Thieppe districts in the same department.

Thousands ⁠of people have ⁠died in recent years attempting to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from West Africa, including ‌635 in the first five months of this year, according to ‌migrant rights ‌group Walking Borders

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals. Since the start of November, El Hierro authorities said more than 3,300 people had arrived aboard around 30 boats.

articles.title: 'Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha' actress Shin Min-a quietly donated over $2.7 million in 15 years to help burn victims, underprivileged children and vulnerable families; charity officials initially mistook her recurring contributions for an error
articles.summary: South Korean actor Shin Min-a, best known internationally for her performances in 'Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha', has drawn attention for a charitable record that
articles.body: South Korean actor Shin Min-a, best known internationally for her performances in 'Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha', has drawn attention for a charitable record that spans more than 15 years. The actor has reportedly donated over 3.7 billion won (approximately $2.7 million) during this period, supporting burn victims, children from low-income families and other vulnerable communities. Her contributions came to light after a post attributed to a foundation representative revealed that the organisation initially believed the recurring deposits from her bank account were made by mistake, according to The Korea JoongAng Daily.The post, which circulated across online communities and social media in South Korea, described how substantial amounts of money had begun arriving in an organisation's account every month in 2009. The person claiming to represent the foundation said they initially struggled to identify the source of the deposits before discovering that they were coming from Shin. The representative also claimed that the actor had specifically requested that her contributions not be publicised and that the money be used to pay for burn patients' treatment and support study programmes for children from disadvantaged backgrounds.The Korea JoongAng Daily noted that the foundation representative's exact identity remained unclear. Nevertheless, Shin's longstanding charitable work has been independently documented, with several organisations confirming the donations they have received from her over the years.More than $800,000 donated to burn victims aloneOne of the organisations that has publicly acknowledged Shin's support is the Hallym Burn Foundation, which helps people suffering from serious burn injuries. According to SBS, the actor has donated 100 million won (approximately $73,000) to the organisation every year since 2015. Her contributions reached 1.1 billion won (around $800,000) by September 2026, marking 11 consecutive years of annual donations.The foundation said the money has helped cover medical treatment and nursing expenses for burn victims, particularly children and women. More than 200 patients have benefited from the financial assistance made possible by her contributions.According to an official from the Hallym Burn Foundation quoted by SBS, Shin makes an effort to find out what young patients would like to receive during Christmas and traditional holidays. She surveys the children about their wishes and arranges personalised gifts for them. In some instances, she has also sent handwritten letters along with the presents, while in others she has delivered the gifts personally. The foundation said her support over more than a decade had been deeply appreciated, particularly because it continued without her seeking publicity or recognition.From vulnerable children to disaster-hit communitiesAccording to The Korea JoongAng Daily, 'The Remarried Empress' actress has supported disadvantaged children, older adults living alone and North Korean defectors since 2009. She has also contributed to emergency relief efforts following natural disasters and other crises across South Korea. Her donations have reportedly supported people affected by the Covid-19 pandemic, wildfires, earthquakes and floods. The actor has continued to contribute whenever communities have faced emergencies, making disaster relief another important part of her philanthropic work.The recent reports also highlighted her support for educational programmes and study facilities for children from low-income households. Such initiatives can provide children with access to learning resources and a suitable environment to study, particularly when their families cannot afford additional educational support.Although the reported 3.7 billion won figure attracted attention, The Korea JoongAng Daily said her cumulative charitable contributions are believed to have crossed 4 billion won (approximately $2.9 million) when earlier and additional donations are included.Donated on her wedding day tooShin's commitment to charitable giving also continued during a significant personal milestone. On her wedding day in December 2025, she and fellow South Korean actor Kim Woo-bin donated a combined 300 million won (approximately $220,000) to three organisations, including the Hallym Burn Foundation, Asan Medical Center and Good Friends, according to SBS.Kim, who has also maintained a record of charitable contributions since 2014, has reportedly donated more than 1.1 billion won over the years. Together, the couple's cumulative donations have exceeded 5 billion won (approximately $3.6 million), according to The Korea JoongAng Daily.Shin has previously spoken about why she did not want her charitable activities to become public knowledge. She said she once believed that good deeds should be done quietly, without attracting attention. However, she later came to feel that when influential people speak about their contributions, it can encourage others to participate in charitable activities as well.In an earlier interview, she expressed the hope that her support would reach people who might otherwise be left without assistance. She also said she hoped that reports about donations could inspire even one person to think about helping someone in need.Shin Min-a's return to the screenThe renewed attention around Shin's philanthropy comes as the actor returns to the screen with the Disney+ original series The Remarried Empress, released on November 4, 2026. She plays Navier, a queen whose marriage and position are challenged after her husband seeks to replace her with another woman.Shin has built a successful career through popular South Korean television dramas, including 'Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha', 'Our Blues' and 'My Girlfriend Is a Gumiho'.You use AI every day. articles.title: After a Florida woman reduced her teaching pay from about $49,450 to $20,000, her divorce court denied alimony and gave her husband all parenting time; an appeals court ordered a fresh review of support and parenting
articles.summary: A Florida divorce case involving a teacher who reduced her pay from about $49,450 to $20,000 has been sent back for a new review of alimony, child support
articles.body: A Florida divorce case involving a teacher who reduced her pay from about $49,450 to $20,000 has been sent back for a new review of alimony, child support and parenting arrangements. In Rebecca Zalkin v. Jeffrey Zalkin, the Fourth District Court of Appeal found that the Broward County trial court failed to make legally required findings before denying the wife’s request for alimony and before awarding the husband all timesharing and sweeping decision-making authority. The appellate court reversed parts of the divorce judgment, vacated later amendments made while the appeal was pending, and sent the case back for further proceedings, as per report by Justia U.S Law.The ruling does not decide that the wife is automatically entitled to alimony or that the parents must share time equally. Instead, it holds that the trial court must redo key parts of its analysis using the parties’ net incomes, evidence-based income figures and the proper legal standards for parental responsibility. The court did affirm the denial of the wife’s request for attorney’s fees and costs. Read more about it here:A marriage, two children and a costly career changeRebecca and Jeffrey Zalkin married in 2004 and had two minor children during the marriage. Their divorce case included disputes over alimony, child support, parental responsibility and timesharing, and the parties later agreed on a plan for dividing their property.The wife had worked as a teacher before moving into a teacher’s assistant position during the 2020 to 2021 school year. Evidence at trial showed that the change reduced her salary from $49,449.60 to $20,000. She and her therapist testified that teaching had caused her significant stress, and she said she did not intend to return to a teaching job or leave her current school.The trial court found that she had voluntarily underemployed herself. But the appellate court said that finding alone did not justify the income the judge assigned to her for support purposes.Why the alimony denial was reversedFlorida law requires a trial court to first make specific factual findings about whether a spouse seeking alimony has an actual need for it and whether the other spouse has the ability to pay. Those findings must be based on each party’s net monthly income, calculated by subtracting monthly expenses from net monthly income.The Fourth District found that the trial court did not make those required findings before considering the statutory alimony factors. It also said the court improperly relied on the wife’s imputed gross income rather than making the necessary net-income analysis.The appellate court further held that the trial court should have considered the husband’s voluntary contributions to his 401(k) retirement account when assessing his ability to pay. On remand, the judge must reconsider alimony through a complete need-and-ability-to-pay analysis based on the parties’ net incomes.The problem with imputing incomeA Florida court can impute income to a spouse, but only when the evidence supports both employability and the availability of suitable work. The court must base its conclusion on the person’s employment history, qualifications and probable earnings under prevailing wages, rather than speculating about what might happen later.Here, the appellate court accepted that the wife was voluntarily underemployed, given her education, work history and testimony that she did not intend to return to teaching. But it found no evidence that a teaching position for which she qualified was actually available at the time of trial.The school representative testified that a teacher with a master’s degree currently earned $54,000, but the wife’s last teaching salary was lower than that amount. Because no qualifying teaching job was shown to be open, the appellate court concluded that the $54,000 imputed salary was not supported by competent evidence.The court also rejected the trial court’s imputation of investment income from retirement assets. While a court may consider penalty-free withdrawals that do not invade principal, the trial court made no finding that the assumed withdrawals would leave the retirement principal intact.Gifts and a supportive relationship still matterThe appellate court did not erase every financial consideration raised at trial. It upheld the trial court’s credibility finding that money the wife received from her father was a continuing gift rather than a loan, based on his testimony that he intended to keep supporting her and had no repayment plan.The court also upheld the finding that the wife’s relationship with her boyfriend was a supportive relationship. Florida law allows a judge to consider such a relationship as one factor relevant to equity and justice in an alimony case.Even so, the reversal means those issues must be reconsidered as part of the full net-income analysis on remand. The appellate court made clear that evidence of gifts or a supportive relationship does not replace the required findings about need and ability to pay.Child support must be recalculatedThe wife also challenged the child support award, and the appellate court agreed that it required reconsideration. Because the trial court’s income imputation was unsupported, the child support calculation built on that income also could not stand.The court identified two additional problems. It said the calculation failed to account for the wife’s detriment-related expenses, and it did not properly address the change in support obligations after the older child’s entitlement ends.The case was therefore remanded so the trial court can recalculate child support with evidence-based income figures, relevant expenses and the correct treatment of the children’s changing circumstances.Why all parenting time required a redoThe original final judgment gave the husband 100 percent of timesharing and shared parental responsibility, while also giving him ultimate decision-making authority over all aspects of the children’s lives. At the end of the same judgment, however, it inconsistently stated that the husband had sole parental responsibility.The Fourth District said that giving one parent unlimited decision-making authority effectively nullified shared parental responsibility. Under Florida law, a court may give one parent ultimate authority only over specific issues where the parents cannot agree, rather than handing over control of every area of a child’s life.More importantly, the appellate court held that a judge cannot award sole parental responsibility based only on the best-interest factors. The court must also determine whether shared parental responsibility would be detrimental to the child. Because no such detriment finding appeared in the original judgment, the parenting ruling was reversed.A jurisdictional misstep after the appealAfter the wife filed her appeal, the husband asked the trial court to make the temporary timesharing schedule permanent. The trial court then amended the final judgment to make the parenting plan permanent, clarify that the husband had sole parental responsibility, and add the detriment findings needed to support that award.The appellate court said the trial court lacked jurisdiction to make those substantive changes after the notice of appeal was filed. Once an appeal begins, the lower court is generally divested of authority to alter the order being appealed.The court therefore vacated the amended final judgment. The result is that the husband’s all-timesharing arrangement and sole parental responsibility award do not remain final while the case returns to the trial court for a legally proper review.What happens nextThe Fourth District affirmed only the denial of the wife’s request for attorney’s fees and costs, finding that the trial court properly considered the parties’ relative finances and concluded that the husband lacked the ability to pay.On remand, the trial court must reconsider alimony and child support using net incomes and evidence-supported imputation, recalculate child support with the required adjustments, and revisit parental responsibility and timesharing under the proper legal framework. The appellate court’s message was not that the wife must win, but that the earlier decisions rested on incomplete findings and legal errors.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Gulf War veteran left homeless after heart surgery details how he rebuilt his life from 'square one'
articles.summary: Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. shares his fight to rebuild his life after heart surgery as Fox Corporation and U.S.VETS partner on the "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign.
articles.body: Gulf War veteran Thomas Garrett Jr. returned home to celebratory parades, but years later, he found himself homeless after undergoing heart surgery. Garrett’s efforts to rebuild his life after becoming homeless are highlighted in Fox Corporation’s sixth annual "Make Camo Your Cause" campaign with U.S.VETS, a nationwide initiative ahead of Veterans Day aimed at helping end veteran homelessness. "The homecoming was a phenomenal event," Garrett said Saturday on "Fox News Live." "I became homeless after having heart surgery. So that changed everything about my dynamic in life," he added. AMERICA'S WOUNDED, STRUGGLING VETERANS GET BRAND-NEW HOMES BUILT BY FLORIDA TEENS U.S.VETS, a national nonprofit dedicated to ending veteran homelessness, provides housing, food and career help to service members in need. According to the organization, it assists more than 20,000 veterans and their families each year. To date, U.S.VETS has served over 500,000 meals, provided 418,000 nights of shelter and placed 3,000 veterans into permanent housing. Quandrea Patterson, executive director of U.S.VETS, explained that Garrett’s experience reflects a broader challenge facing veterans as they transition from military to civilian life. NEW YORK JETS OWNER WOODY JOHNSON TO BE HONORED AT TUNNEL TO TOWERS GALA FOR DECADE-LONG PARTNERSHIP "A lot of times when veterans are in service, they're told, and they know exactly what to do because they're mission-focused," Patterson said. "And then during that transition from active service to civilian service or veteran status, a lot of the information, a lot of the things to expect are unknown." The uncertainty surrounding that transition can leave veterans vulnerable to homelessness, Patterson said. For Garrett, U.S.VETS offered the structure and support he needed to move forward. "U.S.VETS is a new starting point for veterans," Garrett said. "It's a square one to where you can build up your life the way the veteran themselves need it. It gives us good structure. It gives us a good routine to begin and to build from there." articles.title: ELAINE PARKER: Democrat win is a wake-up call for Republicans, not a vote for socialism
articles.summary: Midterm elections sent a clear message on affordability, but Democrats would be wrong to interpret their victories as a mandate for socialism.
articles.body: The American people sent a clear message in Tuesday's midterm elections. But Democrats would be making a serious mistake if they interpreted their victories as an endorsement of socialism. Voters weren't demanding bigger government. They wanted relief from the affordability crisis. Republicans shouldn't dismiss the results as a typical midterm setback either. The coalition that delivered President Donald Trump the White House and Republican control of Congress in 2024 expected results. MEHEK COOKE: REPUBLICANS FAILED THE AFFORDABILITY TEST. THIS IS HOW TO WIN VOTERS BACK The voters who hired Republicans to fix the affordability crisis are now holding them accountable for failing to deliver. Americans were tired of inflation, unaffordable housing and watching their paychecks buy less. They believed Republicans would make their lives better. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS But somewhere between winning and governing, Republicans lost control of that message. Trump had a legitimate argument for tariffs: rebuilding American manufacturing and bringing back jobs lost under decades of trade policies, including NAFTA, signed by President Bill Clinton. But Republicans never adequately explained the long-term benefits. Voters heard about tariffs while worrying about higher prices. The same communications failure plagued the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Republicans made lower individual tax rates permanent, restored immediate expensing for qualifying business investments and prevented trillions in scheduled tax increases. Yet how many Americans could explain what that legislation actually did for them? What good is passing legislation that helps working families and small businesses if you can't explain how it makes their lives better? Healthcare was another squandered opportunity. When enhanced COVID-19-era Obamacare subsidies expired, Republicans could have offered a serious affordability alternative built around price transparency, competition and consumer choice. Instead, they surrendered the conversation. Healthcare is part of the affordability crisis. Families don't separate their mortgage, groceries, insurance premiums and deductibles into political categories. It all comes from the same paycheck. Perhaps the biggest warning came from Hispanic voters. The voters who hired Republicans to fix the affordability crisis are now holding them accountable for failing to deliver. Trump made historic gains in 2024 by speaking to their economic aspirations, entrepreneurial spirit and desire for safe communities. Following Trump's 2024 victory, his pollster, John McLaughlin, observed that Republicans had rented the Hispanic vote and warned they needed to work to keep it. Unfortunately, they acted as though they owned it. FLORIDA CONGRESSMAN DIAGNOSES GOP'S BLUE TSUNAMI LOSSES: 'WE FAILED TO MAKE THEM THINK WE CARED ABOUT THEM' Economic frustration drove much of the erosion in support, but immigration enforcement contributed. Trump promised to secure the border and prioritize dangerous criminals. Instead, broader enforcement created fear in Hispanic communities, including among those who supported stronger border security. Republicans worked hard to win those voters in 2024 and then seemingly forgot what brought them into the Republican column. They failed to maintain that trust, much less expand it. My home state of Florida should be a wake-up call. Republicans can celebrate electing Byron Donalds as Florida's first Black governor and holding major statewide offices. But Donalds narrowly defeated David Jolly despite a roughly 1.5-million Republican voter-registration advantage. That advantage provided a cushion against the national Democratic swing, not immunity from it. Those margins should concern Republican leaders. Then there's the war with Iran. Whatever the administration's strategic justification, it failed to make a compelling case to Americans already struggling financially. Voters saw higher gasoline prices without a clearly articulated reason for the conflict. None of this gives Democrats a mandate to push socialist policies. A vote against Republican performance isn't necessarily a vote for higher taxes, more government spending or expanded bureaucracy. Many of these same voters supported Trump just two years ago because they wanted a different economic direction. Democrats have earned an opportunity to address affordability, not a blank check for an ideological agenda. Republicans, meanwhile, need to reconnect their policies to the people they're supposed to serve. Lower taxes, stronger small businesses, affordable healthcare and greater economic opportunity remain a compelling agenda. But voters need to see and feel the benefits. Following Trump's 2024 victory, his pollster, John McLaughlin, observed that Republicans had rented the Hispanic vote and warned they needed to work to keep it. Unfortunately, they acted as though they owned it. Tuesday's election was not a mandate for socialism. It was a demand for affordability, accountability and results. articles.title: Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa plans faceless anti-terror courts: Report
articles.summary: Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province plans to set up faceless anti-terrorism courts to protect witnesses, prosecutors and judges involved in terrorism
articles.body: Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province plans to set up faceless anti-terrorism courts to protect witnesses, prosecutors and judges involved in terrorism cases, according to a report by Dawn on Sunday.The provincial administration also plans to allocate 70 billion Pakistani rupees annually to the police and Counter-Terrorism Department to strengthen their capabilities, the report said.The developments come less than a month after Pakistan's federal government imposed emergency and governor's rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, accusing the provincial government led by former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) of failing to engage in the fight against terrorism.Under the move, the chief minister and provincial cabinet ceased to hold office, with Governor Faisal Karim Kundi assuming executive authority with the assistance of an 11-member advisory council.Both the national assembly and senate approved the emergency on October 14, while a joint sitting of Parliament endorsed the emergency and governor's rule the following day.At a televised briefing on Sunday, Home Secretary Amjad Ali Khan said an amendment had been sent to establish faceless anti-terrorism courts. He said witnesses were reluctant to testify in terrorism cases because of fears for their safety. The proposed system would also protect prosecutors and judges, *Dawn* quoted him as saying.Khan said the administration planned to allocate 59.8 billion Pakistani rupees to the police and 10.3 billion Pakistani rupees to the Counter-Terrorism Department, with funds earmarked for infrastructure and equipment.The plans also include strengthening police stations and checkpoints, expanding the Safe City project and installing anti-drone systems in Dera Ismail Khan, Lakki Marwat and Bannu, the report said.Khan said the province faced a shortage of more than 10,000 police personnel and lacked adequate security infrastructure, particularly in the merged districts. He also flagged weak counter-drone capabilities, noting that militants were increasingly using drone technology.The administration plans to intensify intelligence-based operations, arrest terrorist facilitators, re-verify people placed on Pakistan's Fourth Schedule and mobilise the Rapid Response Force, Khan said.It also plans to deploy artificial intelligence tools to monitor social media and counter terrorist narratives, while satellite communication systems will be installed in areas with inadequate connectivity.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governor Kundi, who attended the briefing, said restoring peace and strengthening the police were the administration's priorities. He said development could follow only after security was restored and called for greater political ownership of the fight against terrorism.Kundi said the police would be provided with weapons, ammunition and other resources, while facilities in the merged districts would also be improved. He said groups taking up arms against the state could not be offered dialogue and would be dealt with accordingly, Dawn reported.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
