articles.title: ROBERT L MAGINNIS: Iran War cost Republicans Congress. What will it cost America?
articles.summary: JD Vance blamed the Middle East conflict for Republican losses as Democrats flipped both houses of Congress after eight months of fighting Iran.
articles.body: Twenty years ago, American voters punished Republicans over an unpopular war in the Middle East. On Nov. 3, they did it again. In 2006, it was Iraq. This time, it was Iran. Democrats captured both houses of Congress, flipping at least seven Senate seats, including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa. Vice President JD Vance put the blame squarely where President Donald Trump would rather not have it: on the war his administration launched eight months ago. I remember the earlier debacle. As a Pentagon strategist during the run-up to the 2003 Iraq invasion, I attended meetings with Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld and senior military leaders. I questioned whether the administration had adequately considered what would follow Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s overthrow. HUGH HEWITT: THE GHOSTS OF 2006 ARE STIRRING — BUT WILL THEY CATCH THE GOP? Now Trump faces a reckoning of his own. American forces have inflicted tremendous damage on Iran’s military. But military success does not guarantee strategic success, especially when the American people lose confidence in the mission. Vance was blunt in his Nov. 4 assessment: "The reason we lost is the war." He dared anyone to argue that "losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it." VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY' Trump acknowledged that the war contributed to Republican losses but defended his decision: "I would have done nothing differently." He added, "You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He is right about that. But the election raises a question his administration has yet to answer: What has eight months of fighting accomplished that will last? TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME I have consistently argued that a nuclear-armed Iran is unacceptable. In June 2025, I supported decisive action against Tehran’s deeply buried Fordow nuclear facility. Four days later, however, I challenged claims that Iran was only weeks away from producing a usable nuclear weapon. The intelligence did not publicly establish that conclusion. Those positions were consistent. Iran presented a serious threat, but military action demanded honest intelligence, limited objectives and an understanding of the consequences. Three days before Trump launched Operation Epic Fury on Feb. 28, I warned in Fox News Digital that the administration needed to establish the facts before committing America to another Middle Eastern conflict. I never doubted that American forces could overwhelm Iran’s military. I doubted that Washington had a realistic plan for what came afterward. Eight months later, Washington still lacks a convincing answer, and the political consequences have become impossible to ignore. The Fox News Voter Poll explains much of the Republican defeat. More than a third of voters called the Iran war crucial to their House vote, and about 6 in 10 said attacking Iran was the wrong decision. FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR In a separate Fox News survey, nearly twice as many preferred ending military involvement to lower gasoline prices as favored renewed attacks to stop Iran's nuclear program. That finding should trouble the White House. Americans did not necessarily dismiss the Iranian threat. Many simply concluded that the costs of confronting it had become too high. Now Trump faces a reckoning of his own. American forces have inflicted tremendous damage on Iran’s military. But military success does not guarantee strategic success, especially when the American people lose confidence in the mission. The costs are staggering. A Pentagon estimate submitted to Congress put war spending at $47.1 billion through Oct. 16, a figure that excludes repairs to damaged American bases. As I documented Nov. 4, investigations by the Associated Press and The Wall Street Journal exposed extensive damage to American installations throughout the Middle East. The Journal put the repair bill at $5 billion to $15 billion. Congress must determine what was lost, whether some losses were preventable and what restoring our defenses will cost. COST OF IRAN WAR EXPLODES AS TOLL ON US AIR FLEET NEARLY DOUBLES Then there is the opportunity cost. In August, I examined the Pentagon's decision to divert the Japan-based USS George Washington from the Pacific to the Middle East. That decision reduced America's carrier presence in a region where China poses our greatest long-term military challenge. A carrier committed to confronting Iran is unavailable for operations in the western Pacific. That is a strategic tradeoff Washington cannot afford to overlook. TRUMP IS WINNING EVERY BATTLE IN IRAN—AND RISKING THE WAR THAT MATTERS China remains America’s principal strategic competitor, and every commitment to Iran must be weighed against that reality. In 1974, as a young lieutenant in South Korea, I served in then-Lt. Col. Colin Powell’s battalion. Powell later championed a doctrine that stressed clear objectives, overwhelming force, public support and an exit strategy. In my July Fox column, I questioned whether Washington was honoring those principles in Iran. Tuesday’s election exposed the consequences of neglecting one of them: A president cannot sustain a costly war indefinitely without the support of the American people. AMERICANS 'FRUSTRATED' ABOUT IRAN WAR GOING INTO MIDTERMS AS TRUMP ADMIN HAS DECISION TO MAKE: GOP LAWMAKER Instead of the short campaign Trump promised, America has spent eight months cycling through strikes, ceasefires and negotiations that have produced no durable settlement. Iran has suffered enormously. The opening strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and devastated important military installations, yet the regime survives. Its nuclear ambitions remain unresolved and Tehran continues threatening commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Eight months of military punishment have weakened Iran, but they have not produced the durable settlement Americans were led to expect. None of this counsels surrender to Tehran. America needs a strategy capable of achieving something more lasting than another round of destruction. In January, Democrats can investigate military losses, demand testimony from Pentagon leaders, impose conditions on appropriations and challenge the administration’s authority to continue fighting. Trump retains considerable executive power, but congressional resistance could complicate nearly every national security initiative of his final two years. Tehran is already celebrating. Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, declared that "Americans said NO TO WAR." That is precisely the conclusion Washington must not encourage. Beijing and Moscow will also be watching to see whether the Iran war has weakened America's ability to sustain its commitments elsewhere. The day after the 2006 election, President George W. Bush announced that Rumsfeld would be replaced by Robert Gates. Two months later, he announced a new Iraq strategy built around a troop surge, and Gen. David Petraeus, whose counterinsurgency expertise I publicly supported, took command. Trump may face similar pressure to replace Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or other senior advisors. Their assessments of Iranian capabilities and protection of American forces deserve scrutiny. But new faces alone will accomplish little unless the president also rethinks the strategy itself. The administration is already divided over what comes next. Axios reported that Vance and presidential envoy Steve Witkoff favor pursuing an agreement, while Hegseth and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu support renewed military action. Other senior advisors favor continued economic pressure. Trump must decide among those competing approaches, but only after establishing which one offers America a realistic prospect of lasting security. Trump needs experienced advisors willing to challenge his assumptions, an honest accounting of the war’s costs and a fresh assessment of how closely American decisions should follow Israel’s preferences. Our interests overlap, but they are not identical. Above all, he must decide what victory means. Is it preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, protecting regional shipping, negotiating a durable settlement or removing the regime? Those goals demand very different commitments, and Americans deserve to know which their president intends to pursue. The Fox News Voter Poll explains much of the Republican defeat. More than a third of voters called the Iran war crucial to their House vote, and about 6 in 10 said attacking Iran was the wrong decision. For now, Trump appears reluctant to resume major attacks while diplomatic efforts continue. That gives him an opportunity to reconsider his approach before another round of fighting imposes still greater costs. He should use it. Twenty years ago, voters forced Washington to reconsider a costly war. They have delivered another warning. Their commander in chief now owes them, and the American people, a credible plan to finish the mission at a price this country is willing to pay. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ROBERT MAGINNIS

articles.title: At least four dead and dozens injured after trains collide in Egypt
articles.summary: A collision outside Giza caused carriages to derail, with a massive emergency operation under way.
articles.body:
A train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza has killed four people and injured at least 88, the health ministry has said.

Egypt's railway authority said a train travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan.

Images from the scene showed several carriages had derailed and fallen down an embankment.

The Egyptian health ministry said at least 72 ambulances were sent, while local media reported a train driver was among the dead.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he was following the incident with "great concern" and extended his "deepest condolences to the families of those who lost their lives".

"I have directed state agencies to provide the necessary medical care, promptly investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent," he wrote on X.

The government said hospitals in the area had been out "on heightened alert" as they coped with a massive influx of patients.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region have been suspended, BBC Arabic reported.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat.

The rail authority dispatched emergency teams and cranes to the scene.

Al-Ayyat is the site of Egypt's worst-ever rail disaster, when a fire on a train killed more than 370 people in 2002.

articles.title: An Ohio homeowner refused to pay for basement walls after spotting defects in a 2021 project; judges said the foundation was structurally sound despite cosmetic flaws and upheld a $45,806 payment to the contractor
articles.summary: An Ohio homeowner who refused to pay for a newly built concrete foundation after noticing visible defects has been ordered by an appeals court to pay the
articles.body: An Ohio homeowner who refused to pay for a newly built concrete foundation after noticing visible defects has been ordered by an appeals court to pay the contractor $45,806. The judges found that the basement walls were structurally sound, even though they had some cosmetic flaws. The dispute began with a residential construction agreement signed in 2021 for the installation of new concrete basement walls. After the concrete was poured, the homeowner refused to make the final payment. The owner argued that the visible defects made the foundation unacceptable and meant the contractor had failed to meet the terms of the agreement. However, an Ohio appeals court upheld the lower court's decision in favour of the contractor. The judges found that the builder had completed most of the agreed work to an acceptable standard. Under Ohio contract law, cosmetic problems do not allow a homeowner to refuse payment when the structure is safe and meets building standards. According to a legal report published by Laws.com, the appeals court upheld the $45,806 payment awarded to the contractor for the completed work, with small deductions allowed for minor repairs that did not affect the structure.Dispute over cosmetic imperfections and structural integrityThe disagreement began shortly after the basement walls were poured in 2021. The homeowner noticed several visible problems on the surface of the new concrete walls. The homeowner argued that surface marks, honeycombing and an uneven finish showed poor workmanship and reduced the value of the property. Believing the work did not meet acceptable standards, the owner stopped making payments and demanded that the contractor either repair or completely replace the basement walls. The contractor disagreed with these claims. The builder argued that the concrete had been poured using accepted construction methods and that the foundation was strong enough to safely support the house. After both sides failed to reach an agreement, the contractor filed a lawsuit to recover the unpaid $45,806 under the construction contract. During the trial, both sides presented engineering reports and expert opinions about the condition of the concrete walls. Inspectors confirmed that the walls had some minor appearance-related problems. However, independent structural assessments found that the basement walls met local building codes and had enough strength to support the weight of the house.Substantial performance and legal standards under Ohio lawWhen reviewing the case, the appeals court focused on the legal rule known as substantial performance, which is used to decide construction payment disputes in Ohio. Under Ohio law, a contractor who completes a project in good faith and delivers its main purpose is generally entitled to payment, even if some minor defects or differences remain. A homeowner can only justify withholding the full payment if they prove that the builder seriously failed to meet the contract terms and did not provide the main benefit promised. As explained in the report by Laws.com, the appeals court said that the main purpose of a basement foundation is to provide structural support for the house. Since technical inspections showed that the walls were safe and structurally sound, the judges considered the visible defects minor and not serious enough to count as a major contract failure. The court explained that homeowners may be allowed to deduct the cost of fixing minor cosmetic problems from the amount owed. However, they cannot refuse to pay the entire remaining balance when the foundation is safe and doing its intended job.Final judgment upholding the contractor payoutThe appeals court upheld the lower court's decision and ordered the homeowner to pay the contractor the outstanding balance of $45,806. The judges said that allowing homeowners to refuse payment because of appearance-related problems that do not affect safety or strength would unfairly harm builders who have completed the main requirements of a construction contract. The decision supports existing legal rules followed by courts across Ohio. It makes a clear distinction between minor surface defects and serious structural problems in residential construction disputes. It also confirms that a foundation that meets safety and building requirements cannot be rejected solely because its appearance is not perfect.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
